moTa: Throughout the seventh lunar month, An Nhiên Pagoda opens the Vu Lan season of gratitude to parents. It is a time to thank our parents, pin on a rose, float a lantern for loved ones who have passed, share a simple vegetarian meal and do small good deeds. Animal release here comes with care: right species, right place, no harm to nature. If the month has only 29 days, the season ends on the 29th.

loiChao.noiDung: Vu Lan season is here. Have you checked in on your parents today?
An Nhiên Pagoda welcomes you in this month of gratitude to parents.
A small rose is waiting at the pagoda gate for you to pin on.
Hello. Sit down for a moment and remember those who have loved you.
Seventh-month drizzle has dampened the yard. Walk slowly, friend.
You're invited to float a lantern on the lotus pond tonight.
In this season of filial love, may your day with loved ones be gentle.
The pagoda kitchen is cooking vegetarian rice. Come share a simple meal.
Hello. Is there a thank-you you've been saving for too long?
Peaceful Vu Lan! May your family be warm and full of love.
The evening bell just rang. Share a minute of gratitude for your parents.
The season of remembrance has come. The pagoda always keeps a place for it.

thongDiep.noiDung: Honoring your parents need not wait until you succeed. A meal with them today already honors them.
Ask your mother what her favorite dish is. She may have spent a lifetime cooking yours and forgotten her own.
The rose pinned on during Vu Lan is a gentle reminder: a parent's love always stays close to the heart.
If your parents have passed, hold on to one good thing they taught you and live it each day. That is the rose that lasts the longest.
Call your father for no reason at all. Just to ask whether he has eaten today.
Remembering those who have passed isn't about endless sorrow, but about keeping the good they gave.
A simple vegetarian meal lightens the body and settles the heart. Eat slowly, grateful for every grain.
Release animals wisely: choose native species, return them to the right habitat, and never buy animals caught just to be freed.
Never release pet fish, red-eared sliders or other non-native species into rivers and lakes. Love one creature without harming the whole stream.
Sometimes the finest release is never catching, caging or harming any animal in the first place.
Tell the children about their grandparents. A story retold is how those before us stay beside us.
Loving your parents also means caring for yourself, because your health is their peace of mind.
Seventh-month rains are here. Holding an umbrella for an elder crossing the street is a small good deed.
Apologize to your parents for a time you spoke harshly. Parents have often forgiven long ago and are only waiting for you to speak.
Lanterns drift on the water, carrying remembrance away and leaving peace behind.
Some people are like second parents: teachers, caregivers, mentors. Remember them this season too.
Find an old family photo. Looking at those smiles from long ago, the heart softens.
A good deed this Vu Lan can be very small: pour a cup of water, share a meal, ask after someone who is lonely.
Listening closely as your parents tell an old story for the tenth time is also an act of devotion.
If you still hold anger toward your parents, give yourself time. Understanding is a long road, walked step by step.
Cook a simple vegetarian dish for the family. A meal you cook is a gift your parents remember for a long time.
Light a lamp for those who have passed, then light a smile for those still beside you.
Remembrance is saying thank you to everyone who passed through your life, even those you could not say goodbye to.
Send your siblings a message. Parents are happiest when they see their children caring for one another.
Red rose or white, each one is love. No one is without a rose of their own.
Tidy the family altar and wipe your grandparents' photo frame. That small act brings you closer to them.
To help animals, you can support a rescue center, pick up litter by the river or plant another tree.
Our parents' hair grays a little each day without us noticing. Today, take a long look at their hands.
Devotion isn't measured in gifts but in presence: being there in joy and being there in illness.
Vu Lan season is closing, but thanking your parents need not wait until next year.

loiNguyen.noiDung: May my parents be healthy, eat well, sleep soundly and live happily with their children.
I send my gratitude to my mother, who stayed awake so many nights for me.
I thank my father, a man of few words who loved me quietly.
I remember my late grandparents with love, respect and peace.
May my loved ones who have passed be remembered through all the good they did.
This month I vow to spend more time with my parents.
I vow to eat vegetarian one day a week, so my heart grows kinder and my body lighter.
I vow to release animals properly, without harming rivers, lakes or native species.
May those who have lost their parents find people who love and support them.
I apologize to my parents for the times I was careless, and vow to care more.
I vow to do good deeds during Vu Lan as a way of thanking my parents.
May my teachers and those who guided me always be happy and well.
I vow to live kindly so my parents can be at ease, whether I am near or far.
May those caring for sick parents find more strength and people to share the load.
May my grief for those who have passed slowly turn into gratitude.
May my siblings and I learn to give way to each other, so our parents need not be saddened.
I vow to listen to my parents more and speak less in anger.
May all beings live peacefully in their own natural habitats.
I vow to keep the good ways my grandparents left and pass them on to the children.
May elders who live alone be looked in on by family and neighbors this Vu Lan.
I vow to sleep early and eat regular meals so my parents far away worry less about me.
May my mother get more rest after so many years of hard work.
I vow to learn to understand my parents, even the things I didn't understand before.
I send my love to the family member I never got to say goodbye to.
I vow to cook a vegetarian meal with my family and sit down to eat together.
May children separated from their parents soon be reunited with their families.
I vow to plant a tree to remember my grandparents and leave shade for others.
May every parent be loved and respected by their children.
I vow that each time I pin a flower on, I will remind myself to honor my parents.
May my heart after this Vu Lan be softer and more loving toward others.

tho: At Vu Lan I think of those who raised me
Of evening rice and home, so warm and free
The flower on my shirt holds all I owe
A thank-you for the love they chose to show
queDacBiet.loiGiai: A warm evening meal and a roof against sun and rain are so familiar that we rarely remember who carried them. This verse invites you to pause during Vu Lan and see the long road your parents walked for you. The flower on your shirt is only a small sign; what matters is gratitude spoken aloud and shown in deeds, while your parents are there to hear it.
queDacBiet.loiKhuyen: Today, tell your parents or whoever raised you a very specific thank-you for something they did for you.

tho: A lantern drifts along the river's flow
Its quiet light a lotus, pink aglow
I send with it my longing, deep and wide
The sorrow fades, but love stays at my side
queDacBiet.loiGiai: The lantern drifts across the water, carrying your remembrance of loved ones who have passed. This verse doesn't ask you to forget, nor to grieve forever. Longing is sent off gently, while love stays in the way you live each day. Those who have gone far are still present in the good habits, the advice and the smiles they left in you.
queDacBiet.loiKhuyen: Write a few lines about one good thing a departed loved one taught you, then choose a day this week to live it out.

tho: Release a fish into the stream it knows
Its native home, where it belongs and grows
Love every creature, keep the rivers clear
With kindness and with wisdom, joy is near
queDacBiet.loiGiai: Compassion for all creatures is precious, but compassion without understanding can sometimes do harm. This verse reminds you that every species has its own familiar water; releasing the wrong species in the wrong place can upset a whole ecosystem. The finest release is never catching animals to set free, choosing native species and the right place, or simply keeping rivers clean and plants green. Kindness joined with knowledge makes joy complete.
queDacBiet.loiKhuyen: Before doing a good deed, learn a little about it first. This season, try picking up litter by a lake or planting a tree instead of buying fish to release.
